blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Cross-Embodiment Transfer**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol IV, Physical Data, § Cross-Embodiment Transfer
blocks.md: Borrowing manipulation demonstrations from another robot arm looks effortless in tensor space, because both datasets store image frames and seven-element action vectors. That ease disappears when a trajectory recorded on a wide-stroke, \$50\text{ Hz}$ gripper drives a narrower, \$20\text{ Hz}$ gripper into its mechanical endstops or misses a moving conveyor part by centimeters. Physical demonstration trajectories never represent a task in the abstract.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Embodiment contract matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Every trajectory encodes the sensor geometry, timing, kinematic and torque limits, and compliance of the machine that produced it, so range normalization is cosmetic and borrowed data must pass an embodiment gate.

questions.q: The section **Cross-Embodiment Transfer** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Nominally identical units differ in transmission, mounts, and motor constants, so a failed attempt and a failed recording must be told apart per unit.

One command exists as four signals (requested, mapped, enforced, measured) and every pair must be dated at the exposure midpoint, because the tap chosen and the pairing lag decide what behavior the label teaches.

Behavioral cloning's worst-case excess cost grows as T^2*eps because training error is weighted by the expert's occupancy, and labeling learner-visited states makes it linear only while a recovering action still exists.

Every trajectory encodes the sensor geometry, timing, kinematic and torque limits, and compliance of the machine that produced it, so range normalization is cosmetic and borrowed data must pass an embodiment gate.
